Close behind, **Maybe Happy Ending** distinguishes itself as one of the most original musicals in recent years, with critics embracing its unlikely premise—a tender love story between robots—and its genuine emotional resonance.

The current Broadway landscape reflects an impressive range, from bold new voices to beloved classics. **Oh, Mary!**, Cole Escola's absurdist take on Mary Todd Lincoln, brings irreverent comedy to the historical drama, while revivals like **Ragtime** demonstrate how classic musicals can speak powerfully to contemporary audiences. Long-running spectacles including **The Lion King**, **The Book of Mormon**, and **Hadestown** maintain their critical standing, proving their enduring appeal alongside newer arrivals.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across all featured productions, March 2026 represents a particularly strong moment for Broadway quality. The mix includes everything from Julie Taymor's groundbreaking puppetry to the magical stagecraft of **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child**, from the intoxicating Cuban rhythms of **Buena Vista Social Club** to the cynical razzle-dazzle of **Chicago**.

Whether you're drawn to innovative new works or timeless revivals, this month offers exceptional opportunities to experience Broadway at its finest.

With an average critic score of 77/100 across these three productions, March 2026 presents theatergoers with options ranging from intimate comedy to large-scale technical showcases. The show demonstrates how classic musicals can speak directly to contemporary audiences when mounted with care and conviction.

On the opposite end of the theatrical spectrum, **Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York)** proves that modest scale doesn't mean modest rewards. This British import charms reviewers with its sincere performances and heartfelt simplicity, offering theatergoers an intimate alternative to Broadway's typically larger productions. The rom-com's two-hander structure allows for focused character work that critics find genuinely affecting.

Meanwhile, **Chess** generates the most divided response among reviewers. While no one disputes the appeal of the ABBA-penned score or the vocal prowess of its star trio—Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit, and an unnamed Christopher—critics split on whether the production successfully navigates the musical's notoriously complex book and Cold War themes.

With an average critical score of 75 across these three shows, March offers solid if not spectacular options for Broadway audiences seeking everything from epic Americana to quirky romance to pop-operatic spectacle. Whether you're drawn to historical drama, intimate storytelling, or vocal fireworks, this month's new arrivals provide clear entry points for different theatrical tastes.

best-broadway-plays-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of a season abruptly curtailed by the pandemic. These productions, which debuted in those brief pre-shutdown months, range from bold reimaginings of classics to powerful dramatic revivals that have since cemented their place in theater history.

Leading our selection is **Les Misérables**, a grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre that earns an 83/100 from critics. This stripped-down production proves that Cameron Mackintosh's epic still has new stories to tell, even if some purists remain skeptical of the radical approach.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as perhaps the most significant rediscovery of the season, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a revival that scores 78/100. Critics widely celebrate this long-overdue production, which demonstrates how the play's examination of race, power, and identity within a segregated Army base remains devastatingly relevant.

The season also features more divisive work, including Ivo van Hove's **West Side Story**, which reimagines the Bernstein-Sondheim classic with stark video design and unconventional staging choices that split critical opinion. Meanwhile, **My Name is Lucy Barton** showcases Laura Linney in a solo performance that critics universally admire, even when they question the adaptation itself.

With an average score of 74/100 across these five productions, the class of 2020 demonstrates Broadway's continued appetite for both reinvention and rediscovery. Whether you're drawn to ambitious reinterpretations or powerful dramatic revivals, these shows offer compelling reasons to revisit this pivotal moment in theater history.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that premiered in 2021 represent a remarkable period of theatrical renewal. That year marked not just the industry's post-pandemic reopening, but an artistic resurgence that brought experimental forms, bold reimaginings, and urgent voices to center stage.

The strongest productions from this era share a willingness to challenge theatrical conventions. **Dana H.** stands out as perhaps the most audacious, with Deirdre O'Connell delivering an unforgettable performance through lip-syncing to recorded interviews—a technique that critics found mesmerizing despite its unconventional nature. Similarly, **Is This a Room** transforms a verbatim FBI transcript into gripping drama, proving that documentary theater can achieve pulse-pounding intensity.

The year also saw major revivals that reimagined classics for contemporary audiences. **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** earns widespread acclaim for its immersive staging that completely transforms the Playhouse Theatre, while **Company** gains new resonance through its gender-swapped central character. Even **The Phantom of the Opera**, which critics acknowledge as campy and uncool, continues to demonstrate the enduring appeal of Andrew Lloyd Webber's spectacle.

Intimate solo performances also distinguished this season, with **Lackawanna Blues** showcasing Ruben Santiago-Hudson's virtuosic character work and **The Lehman Trilogy** (technically featuring three actors) earning praise as an epic theatrical achievement.

With an average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 Broadway season delivered consistently strong work across genres—from experimental docudrama to crowd-pleasing musicals. Whether you're drawn to theatrical innovation or reimagined classics, these productions offer compelling reasons to explore what made this pivotal year memorable.

best-broadway-plays-2022.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the 2022 Broadway season stands as a remarkable period of theatrical achievement, marked by an impressive concentration of Pulitzer Prize-winning works and daring new voices that reshaped the American stage.

The ten productions featured in this guide maintain an exceptional average critic score of 83/100, reflecting a season where quality consistently trumped spectacle. Leading the pack is **Kimberly Akimbo** (88/100), the quirky musical that critics hailed as a near-perfect gem, expertly balancing humor with profound emotional depth. Close behind, both **Into the Woods** (86/100) and **A Strange Loop** (86/100) demonstrate the season's range—the former a stripped-down Sondheim revival that serves as a triumphant tribute to the late composer, the latter a brazenly original meta-musical that earned both Pulitzer recognition and widespread critical acclaim for its brutal honesty.

What distinguishes this collection is its commitment to substantive storytelling. Four Pulitzer Prize-winning plays appear in the lineup—**A Strange Loop**, **Topdog/Underdog**, **Between Riverside and Crazy**, **How I Learned to Drive**, and **Cost of Living**—alongside Tom Stoppard's deeply personal **Leopoldstadt** and Jordan E. Cooper's audacious satire **Ain't No Mo'**. The season proved that Broadway audiences were hungry for work that challenged, provoked, and moved them beyond easy entertainment.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting old favorites, this guide offers a comprehensive look at the shows that defined a pivotal moment in contemporary theater.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the Broadway plays that premiered in 2023 continue to demonstrate the enduring power of theatrical storytelling, with several productions maintaining their cultural relevance more than two years after their debuts.

The class of 2023 proves particularly strong, averaging an impressive 82/100 across critical reception. Leading the field is Maria Friedman's revival of **Merrily We Roll Along** (85/100), which successfully rehabilitates Stephen Sondheim's infamous 1981 flop into an emotionally resonant triumph. The production shares top honors with **Stranger Things: The First Shadow** (85/100), a West End transfer that surprises critics by transcending its source material with technically stunning stagecraft.

Close behind, **Appropriate** (83/100) earns recognition as a modern masterpiece, with Sarah Paulson anchoring a searing family drama about inherited racism and buried secrets. The year also brings vital revivals that speak to contemporary concerns: **Purlie Victorious** (82/100) finds Ossie Davis's 1961 satire bracingly relevant for modern audiences, while **Parade** (82/100) resonates with urgent timeliness through Ben Platt and Micaela Diamond's powerhouse performances.

The diversity of this collection is notable—from Alex Edelman's solo comedy **Just for Us** (81/100) to the Pulitzer-winning **Fat Ham** (80/100), from the musical textures of **Buena Vista Social Club** (81/100) to the immersive rock drama **Stereophonic** (79/100). These productions represent Broadway at its most varied, offering everything from intimate one-person shows to large-scale spectacles.

Whether you're seeking classic revivals reimagined for contemporary audiences or bold new voices pushing theatrical boundaries, the plays of 2023 offer compelling options still running in 2026.

best-broadway-plays-2024.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in March 2026

As Broadway moves through March 2026, the shows that debuted in 2024 continue to demonstrate remarkable staying power and critical acclaim. This collection of ten productions maintains an impressive average critic score of 83/100, reflecting a particularly strong season for theatrical storytelling across multiple genres.

Leading the field is **Stereophonic**, David Adjmi's immersive rock drama set in a 1970s recording studio, which earns the highest marks at 88/100. Critics consistently praise its authentic portrayal of the creative process and its ability to capture the tension and artistry of making music. Close behind is **Operation Mincemeat**, the grassroots British sensation that successfully made the leap from fringe theater to the West End and now Broadway, earning 87/100 for its inventive energy and ensemble work.

The season showcases notable diversity in form and subject matter. **Maybe Happy Ending** brings an unexpectedly moving robot love story to musical theater, while **Cole Escola's Oh, Mary!** reimagines Mary Todd Lincoln as a cabaret-obsessed narcissist in what critics describe as an absurdist comedic tour de force. Traditional revivals also shine, with Audra McDonald offering a fresh interpretation of Mama Rose in **Gypsy** and a lavish new production of **Oliver!** balancing spectacle with Dickensian grit.

From intimate dramas like **Mary Jane** to ambitious dance-theater hybrids like **Illinoise**, these productions represent Broadway's range at its finest. Whether you're drawn to innovative new works or reimagined classics, this lineup offers compelling reasons to experience live theater this season.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2025

As March 2026 arrives, the Broadway plays that opened throughout 2025 continue to demonstrate the enduring power of dramatic storytelling on stage. This curated collection of ten productions—averaging an impressive 84/100 critic score—showcases the season's range, from bold new works to reimagined classics that resonate with contemporary audiences.

Leading the field is Ivo van Hove's stripped-down revival of **All My Sons** (91/100), which earns widespread critical acclaim for transforming Arthur Miller's classic into a visceral, emotionally devastating experience through minimalist staging and exceptional ensemble work. Close behind, the 20th-anniversary mounting of **The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee** (89/100) proves the musical's surprising staying power, with critics celebrating its airtight construction and emotional authenticity. Meanwhile, **Paddington The Musical** (86/100) charms reviewers with its theatrical ingenuity, particularly the remarkably lifelike bear puppet that anchors this family-friendly adaptation.

The season also highlights significant new American voices. Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer-winning **English** (82/100) earns strong praise for its nuanced exploration of language and identity, while Branden Jacobs-Jenkins delivers another incisive family drama with **Purpose** (82/100). Mona Mansour's **Liberation** (84/100) stands out as an ambitious feminist memory play that critics find both timely and moving, despite some structural reservations.

From David Yazbek's darkly comic **Dead Outlaw** (83/100) to a timely **Ragtime** revival (83/100) anchored by Joshua Henry's powerhouse performance, these productions reflect Broadway's commitment to both artistic innovation and meaningful reexamination of the canon. Whether seeking contemporary relevance or theatrical escapism, audiences have exceptional options to explore this spring.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2026

March 2026 brings a notably lean opening schedule for new Broadway plays, with just one production making its debut this month. While the limited roster reflects the challenging economics facing straight plays on Broadway, the sole entry demonstrates the enduring appeal of well-crafted psychological drama.

**Bug** stands as the month's singular offering, marking the long-awaited Broadway premiere of Tracy Letts' 1996 psychological thriller. With a solid critic score of 74/100 across 35 reviews, the production earns mostly positive notices for its intense exploration of paranoia and delusion. Originally produced by Chicago's Red Orchid Theatre three decades ago, the play arrives on Broadway with renewed relevance, its themes of conspiracy and fractured reality resonating in contemporary discourse. Critics particularly praise the production's claustrophobic staging and committed performances, though some note the material's deliberately unsettling nature may not appeal to all theatergoers.

The sparse March schedule underscores a broader trend in commercial theater, where plays increasingly struggle to secure Broadway berths amid rising production costs and risk-averse producers. That **Bug** makes it to the Great White Way at all speaks to both the strength of Letts' reputation—bolstered by his Pulitzer Prize-winning **August: Osage County**—and the theater community's ongoing commitment to provocative, challenging work.

For audiences seeking substantive dramatic fare this month, **Bug** offers a compelling if confronting option that showcases the raw power of theatrical storytelling. Those planning their spring theater calendar should consider catching this production while monitoring announcements for upcoming play openings in the months ahead.
